item.title: Apprenticeship: practical guide in the Schaffhausen Canton
item.description: How to find an internship position, apprentice salaries, contracts and professional maturity in the Swiss system.

## In a nutshell - The Swiss apprenticeship lasts 2-4 years with alternation between company and vocational school - Salaries vary by canton and sector, progressively increasing during the training course - At the end you get the Federal Professional Certificate (AFP) or the Federal Certificate (CPF)
## Key facts - **What**: Dual vocational training regulated by the Federal Law on Vocational Training (LFPr) - Where: Applied in the Schaffhausen Canton and all 26 Swiss cantons - Duration: 2 years for AFP, 3-4 years for CPF - Who: Managed by cantons and companies, federally supervised by SECO - Degree issued: Certificate of Vocational Training (AFP) or Federal Certificate (CPF)
Apprenticeship is the most common training path for young Swiss people. In Canton Schaffhausen, as in the other 25 cantons, it works according to the dual system: young people alternate days of work in the company with days of lessons at a vocational school. This model guarantees the simultaneous acquisition of practical skills and theoretical knowledge in the classroom.
The duration varies depending on the sector and the level of certification. A federal professional certificate (AFP) takes 2 years, while a federal certificate (CPF) takes 3 or 4 years. Upon completion, the apprentice takes federal exams and attains the nationally recognized degree.

One of the most frequently asked questions is: how much does an apprentice earn? In the Swiss system, salaries vary significantly by canton, sector and year of training. In Canton Schaffhausen, as in the other cantons, there is no uniform federal minimum wage for apprentices — each canton negotiates collective agreements in the various sectors (industry, commerce, crafts, catering, health, education).
Salaries increase from year to year: the first year is the lowest paid, the third and fourth years are the highest. An apprentice in the industrial sector typically earns more than one in the hotel sector. SECO periodically publishes official statistics on the subject, available on the website of the federal agency and on that of the cantonal administration of Schaffhausen.

Finding an internship is a delicate step that requires planning and persistence. In the Canton of Schaffhausen, young people interested can follow a well-tried procedure.
Step 1: Identify the sector and profession
Switzerland recognizes over 250 professions for which it is possible to attend an apprenticeship. Before starting the search, it is essential to choose a consistent sector with your interests (industry, commerce, craftsmanship, catering, healthcare, education, computer science) and your abilities. The SECO and the cantons publish online the complete list of available professions with detailed descriptions of tasks and access requirements.

Online platforms such as job.ch and yousty.ch collect apprenticeship announcements from companies throughout Switzerland, including the Canton of Schaffhausen. It is possible to filter by canton, sector, start year, and level (AFP or CPF). **Step 3: Contact companies directly
Not all companies publish their announcements online. It is possible to send spontaneous applications to companies in the Canton of Schaffhausen in the chosen sector, attaching a CV and school references. A personalized letter that highlights the motivation towards the specific sector increases the chances of receiving a positive response.
Step 4: Contact the cantonal office for vocational training
Each canton, including Schaffhausen, has an office that provides free consultation on apprenticeship paths, lists of authorized companies, and information on cantonal standards. The staff can direct young people towards mentors and specialized guidance figures.
Step 5: Participate in recruitment fairs and initiatives
The Canton of Schaffhausen periodically organizes recruitment fairs, professional fairs, and direct meetings between companies and young people interested. These events are precious opportunities to meet entrepreneurs, ask direct questions, collect information material, and receive internship proposals.
### Timing and deadlines
In the Swiss system, applications for apprenticeships that start in September are generally submitted between January and May of the previous year. item.title: Apprenticeship and vocational training Schaffhausen
item.description: Canton Schaffhausen offers federally contracted apprenticeships. Learn how to find an internship, the rights in a contract, and pathways to professional maturity.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell
- Federal apprenticeship protected by contract: minimum 12 months before the start (CO art. 344-346) - Salaries vary by canton and sector; negotiated between apprentice and employer - Two final certifications: AFC (Professional Training Certificate) and MPC (Professional Maturity) - Cantonal Vocational Training Office manages posts and registrations
## Key facts
- **What**: Internship with employment contract + theoretical training in cantonal vocational school - Where: Companies in the Canton of Schaffhausen + vocational school - When: Average duration 3-4 years, usually beginning of September - Who: Apprentice, employer, school, cantonal office - Requirements: Completion of compulsory schooling, minimum 15 years - Certifications: AFC or MPC, often both - Hours: Maximum 45 hours/week (industry/offices), minimum 4 weeks annual holiday
### The Swiss apprenticeship system in the Canton of Schaffhausen
Apprenticeships in Switzerland are regulated by the Federal Law on Vocational Training (LFPr 2002) and protected by the Code of Obligations (CO art. 344-346). In the canton of Schaffhausen, as in the other cantons, the system follows uniform federal rules, with cantonal management of the training offer and the available places.
A valid internship requires a written contract between apprentice and employer, signed at least 12 months before the actual start. The contract must contain: description of the professional activity, total duration (usually 3-4 years), ## How to find an internship in Schaffhausen
It is essential to start the research **at least 18-24 months before** the end of compulsory schooling. In the canton of Schaffhausen, the cantonal vocational training office maintains a public database of authorised companies and regularly publishes lists of available posts, which can also be consulted through national platforms such as [Annunci di lavoro](nav:jobs).
The main steps of the research:
1. Check the available sectors: metalworking, construction, sales, crafts and logistics are traditionally strong in the canton 2. Contact the cantonal office: free advice and referral to companies in line with interests and skills 3. Consult the company database: identify active employers and their training profiles 4. Apply directly: Submit CV, motivation letter, and school results (there is no federal minimum grade requirement, but many companies evaluate math, languages, and behavior) 5. Participate in cantonal orientation days: the canton organizes annual meetings between candidates and companies
### Required skills and application timeline
Companies evaluate not only school grades, but also practical aptitude, concentration, precision, motivation expressed in the letter, personal hygiene and willingness to attend vocational school 1-2 days/week.
The ideal timeline: 7th year of school (informal research and visits), 8th year (formal applications and
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ## Compensation, apprentice rights and professional maturity
### Salary: formation and variability In Switzerland, there is no federal minimum wage for apprentices; the compensation is negotiated between the employer and the apprentice, often consulting trade union tariffs or local sectoral standards. In the canton of Schaffhausen, the level varies significantly by sector, company size and applicable collective agreements.
**First year**: contained compensation, linked to the initial learning phase. Second and third year: gradual increases according to acquired skills. Fourth year (if provided): approach to the salary of a qualified worker.
The compensation is paid monthly by the employer; the apprentice pays social security contributions (AVS/AI 5.3%, unemployment insurance 1.1%) on the gross salary, like every worker. The canton monitors that levels do not fall below reasonable thresholds, but does not impose uniform minimums.
### Apprentice rights and duties In addition to maximum working hours and minimum holidays, the apprentice has the right to: - Protection of health and safety at work (equipment, training on risks) - Theoretical education in a vocational school without loss of salary for attendance days - Didactic material provided by the school (books, handouts) - Periodic evaluations by the school and the employer to monitor the progress
The duties include: regular attendance at school, work loyalty, respect for company procedures, company confidentiality.
### Professional Maturity: added value for the career During or immediately after the internship, the apprentice can attend the Professional Maturity (MP). In the canton of Schaffhausen, two modalities are offered: integrated MP (1-2 additional afternoons/week during the 3-4 years of the internship) or subsequent MP (1-2 years after obtaining the AFC).
The MP is recognized as equivalent to the federal maturity and allows direct access to the Professional University Schools (SUP) in Switzerland without additional exams. This significantly broadens career prospects.
## Step-by-step procedure: from application to the start of the internship Months 1-6 of the previous year: Active research through [Swiss job announcements](nav:jobs), cantonal database, direct contacts with companies. Preparation of a clear CV and motivational letter.
Months 6-9: Interviews with companies. Possible requests for attitudinal tests, school references, behavioral assessment.
Months 9-12: Signature of the contract (federal obligation: 12 months before the start). Verification that it contains all required clauses.
Three months before the start: Registration with the cantonal vocational school. Employer and canton coordinate administrative procedure.
Start date (usually September): Internship begins. Cantonal registration of the contract in the public archives.
During the internship: School attendance (1-2 days/week), practical work in the company, monthly payment of compensation, periodic evaluations by the school.
Last 6 months: Preparation for the AFC exams (theoretical and practical part). If MP was started, continue in parallel.
End of internship: Obtainment of the AFC certificate. If MP was attended, issue of the federal MP certificate.
### Next steps: how to start concretely If you are interested in an internship in the canton of Schaffhausen, consult [Swiss job announcements](nav:jobs) to see the posts in the sector that interests you. Contact the cantonal office of vocational training (Department of Education) to check specific deadlines, obtain the complete list of companies and receive personalized advice.
Use the [Salary Calculator](nav:calculator) to estimate the cost of living during the internship and plan the monthly budget with the expected compensation. This helps you understand if the compensation is adequate to your financial responsibilities.

item.title: Permit L Schaffhausen: validity, extension and step B
item.description: The L permit allows work for up to 1 year in Switzerland. Learn how to extend it, change employer, and transition to B or C permits in the canton.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Permit L: work up to 1 year in Switzerland, renewable - Valid only at the employer named in the permit - Extension requires confirmation from the employer and new release - Change to B or C possible after specific requirements
## Key facts - **What**: Short-term permit for foreign work - Maximum duration: up to 1 year (renewable) - Competent body: State Secretariat for Migration (SEM), cantonal management - Where: Foreign Office of Canton Schaffhausen - Main constraint: Linked to the employer named in the permit
### What is L Permit
The short-term L permit is the instrument that allows a foreigner to work in Switzerland for a maximum duration of one year. This is not a permanent right: each renewal requires a new request, often conditioned by the employer's willingness to keep you in the workforce. In the canton of Schaffhausen, as in the other Swiss cantons, this permit is managed by the State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) according to federal directives.
Unlike the B residence permit (renewable) or the C residence permit (of longer validity), the L permit is a transitional solution designed for short-term projects, temporary hires or experimental periods of professional integration.
### Validity and renewal
The maximum validity of the L permit is set at one year. This term may be renewed, but each renewal presupposes a ### Conditions for Extension and Renewal
To renew the L permit, it is necessary to initiate the procedure at least two to three months before the expiration date. The Sciaffusa canton usually requires a letter from the employer confirming the continuation of employment, a statement from the worker themselves, and a completed request form. Timing is crucial: a late request may result in a suspension of the permit's validity, making it illegal to continue working until the practice is completed.
A practical aspect not to be overlooked is that renewal is not automatic. If the employer does not wish to continue the employment, the request will be rejected, and you will need to leave the Swiss territory or find a new employer willing to sponsor you for a new request. This creates an administrative dependency: your stay in Switzerland is directly related to your employer's will.
### From Short-Term to Residence Permit
After one or more renewals of the L permit, it is possible to transition to a B residence permit, which has a longer validity period (usually 5 years) and can be renewed without remaining tied to a single employer. The B permit represents a qualitative leap: once obtained, you can change jobs with greater freedom.
Differently is the C domicile permit, which generally requires 10 years of residence in Switzerland, or 5 years if you are a citizen of the European Union or the EEA. The C is the highest level of administrative stability, almost equivalent to an unlimited right of residence.
In the Sciaffusa canton, as in the entire country, the criteria for transitioning from L to B are not fixed by law, but depend on the individual situation (integration, economic situation, absence of administrative problems). The cantonal administration evaluates each case.
### Impact on Work Life and Social Protection
A worker with an L permit must be aware that their status in Switzerland depends on the continuation of employment and the employer's authorization. This influences important choices: taking out a mortgage is more difficult, signing a long-term contract for housing can expose you to risks if the permit is not renewed, and economic planning is complicated by uncertainty.
Remember that you must [register with a health insurance](nav:health) within 3 months of arrival in Switzerland. Health insurance (LAMal) is mandatory for residents and is not negotiable: premiums vary according to age, canton, and deductible chosen, but non-payment results in fines.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Procedure for initial and renewal applications
For initial L permit requests in the canton of Schaffhausen, the steps are:
1. Obtain the job offer from the employer 2. The employer submits the application to the canton of Schaffhausen's foreign office, attaching documentation related to the employment, your CV, and a copy of your passport/identity document 3. The office processes the application and, if everything is in order, issues the L permit valid for up to 1 year 4. You receive the permit via regular mail or collect it directly from the office
For renewal, the process is similar but shorter: the employer submits the application at least 60-90 days before the expiration date, accompanied by a brief report on the work situation and a statement of continued employment. If the report is positive and there are no administrative issues, the renewal is usually granted within 3-4 weeks.
### Expiration and consequences
If the permit expires without renewal, you are required to leave the Swiss territory within the specified deadline. Continuing to work after expiration, even illegally, is punishable by administrative fines and possible expulsion. If you fear that the renewal will not be in time, contact the foreign office immediately to assess whether an extraordinary extension (granted rarely, only for force majeure reasons) is possible.
### Fiscal and contributory implications
During the validity period of the L permit, you are obliged to contribute to Swiss AVS/AI (pension and invalidity, approximately 5.3% as an employee), accident insurance (LAA), and health insurance (LAMal) within 3 months of arrival. If your gross income in Switzerland exceeds a certain threshold (determined annually), you are also subject to federal direct tax, cantonal (the canton of Schaffhausen has its own rates) and municipal taxes.
To evaluate the net impact of a Swiss salary with an L permit, use the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) on the site to simulate tax and contributory deductions and check how much will remain net. This helps you to negotiate the salary knowingly with the employer.
### Find the right job
If you are about to expire the L permit and the current employer cannot renew it, you must find a new job quickly. Consult [our job search engine](nav:jobs) to discover job offers throughout Switzerland. If you know exactly which cantons you want to search, you can refine the search by location and sector.
If you want to plan your future finances beyond the expiration of the L permit and prepare for the transition to B, calculate your total tax burden using the [tax return calculator](nav:tax-return) to anticipate how much you will pay each year.

item.description: Ticino has been a pioneer of European photovoltaics since 1982. Today, ViverTI and Sun Appeal are reinventing residential solar: 2,100 hours of sunshine per year, smart and sustainable homes.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell
- In 1982 Ticino installed the first photovoltaic system in Europe, still operating 44 years later - Ticino enjoys 2,100 hours of sunshine per year: twice as much as Zurich, three times as much as Bern - In the 70s and 80s, more than 60 Ticino homes were already equipped with solar panels
## Key facts

No one asks you the question when you're looking for a home. No real estate agent asking for budget and premises asks you: "Does this house produce energy or consume it?" This is not a marginal issue. It is the heart of a transformation that Ticino, more than other corners of Switzerland, understood decades before the rest of Europe.
In 1982, right here in Ticino, the first photovoltaic system in Europe was connected to the public electricity grid. Not in Germany, where solar dominates the landscape today. Not in Spain, kissed by the Mediterranean. In Ticino. And thatplant still worked today, 44 years later, producing clean energy every single day since 1982. A promise kept. A testimony that solar is not a fleeting experiment but an enduring infrastructure.
But Ticino did not come to photovoltaics by chance. ### From aesthetic problem to integrated design
For years photovoltaics has had a major image problem. It was not a question of technique or cost, but of pure visual aesthetics. The black and bulky solar panels disfigured the facades of the houses. They made houses ugly, at least that was how it was perceived by the buyer. Those who wanted a beautiful house chose the traditional roof. Those who opted for solar paid the price in terms of outward appearance. This dichotomy — sustainability on the one hand, beauty on the other — has long conditioned the residential market, even in Ticino where the sun abounded.
ViverTI and Sun Appeal have decided to reject this compromise. Their vision is not a choice between two lesser evils, a renunciation to be assented to. It is the synthesis: beautiful and sustainable homes, smart and aesthetic, energy-producing and pleasing TO the eye. The design integrates solar as a constituent part of the architecture, not as an exterior accessory. This paradigm shift is possible precisely because Ticino has the ideal geographical context.
With 2,100 hours of sunshine per year, a residential solar system is not a marginal luxury for those who want to feel virtuous. It is a central investment in the economic quality of life of the property. In the 40 years of technical life of a modern plant, it produces continuous, free, clean energy. It is not academic environmental rhetoric: it is concrete domestic economy, family budget.

item.title: Permit L Schaffhausen: validity and extension
item.description: Permit L up to 1 year in Switzerland. In the canton of Schaffhausen, it is renewable and can lead to a residence permit. Conditions, procedures and constraints.
item.content:encoded:
## Brief Overview - Swiss L permit: valid for up to 1 year, renewable - Administered by local cantonal authorities in the Canton of Schaffhausen - Renewal possible; transition to B permit requires established employment - Restrictions tied to declared employer in the request
## Key Facts - **What**: Short-term work permit for foreigners - When: Valid for up to 1 year, renewable upon request - Where: Canton of Schaffhausen, Switzerland - Who: Foreigners primarily from non-EU/EFTA countries - Duration: Maximum 12 months for a single L permit - Renewal: Discretionary, upon request of the employer - Transition: To B permit (residence 5 years) after 24 months - Employer: Worker bound to declared employer
The L permit is a temporary work permit valid for up to 1 year under Swiss legislation on foreign nationals. In the Canton of Schaffhausen, as in all cantons, it is managed by the local migration office according to federal criteria set by the SEM (State Secretariat for Migration).
The L permit allows a foreigner to work for a specific employer for a maximum period of 12 months. It is not renewable automatically for the same position, but can be extended if the employer requests it and the cantonal authorities approve based on local economic conditions and labor market conditions.
In the Canton of Schaffhausen, the procedures for the request and extension follow the federal framework. The Swiss employer must formally submit the request to the cantonal authorities, declaring the expected duration of the employment relationship (up to 1 year).
A fundamental characteristic of the L permit is the binding relationship with the employer. The foreigner cannot change employment without a new authorization. This binding protects the Swiss labor market, reserving priority places for Swiss workers and residents. Any change of employer requires a new request to the cantonal authorities before the worker can start the new employment relationship.
Extension in the Canton of Schaffhausen is possible but not automatic, even if the employer requests it. The authorities assess the occupational, economic, and conduct of the foreign worker during the first permit.
### L Permit versus B and C Permits
The L permit distinguishes itself from the B permit (residence) and the C permit (domicile). The B permit is valid for 5 years and is renewable; the C permit is an indefinite permit of domicile (usually granted after 10 years of residence, 5 years for EU/EFTA citizens under Swiss law). The L permit is the tool for temporary work, while B and C regulate more stable residence. In the Canton of Schaffhausen, the transition from L to B is possible after approximately 24 months of L permit, if the conditions of established employment and integration are met.
As a foreigner in an L permit, your tax obligations follow the same rules as Swiss residents: federal direct tax, cantonal and communal taxes in the Canton of Schaffhausen. Consult the [tax return declaration](nav:tax-return) to understand how to report foreign work income in Switzerland. ## Extension and Conditions in the Canton of Schaffhausen
The extension of the L permit in the Canton of Schaffhausen is subject to specific conditions that vary depending on the labor market situation and the economic needs of the canton. Unlike what is commonly believed, the extension is NOT automatic, even if the employer formally requests it. The cantonal authorities must evaluate various factors before granting the extension.
Firstly, the employer must submit the extension request **before the expiration** of the existing L permit. In the Canton of Schaffhausen, as in the entire Switzerland, a request submitted after the expiration date may be considered inadmissible, resulting in rejection and the need for a new authorization procedure.
Secondly, the cantonal authorities verify the local labor market situation. If the canton has registered high unemployment rates during the period, the extension may be denied, giving priority to Swiss workers and authorized residents. This is a federal criterion applied uniformly in all cantons.
Furthermore, if the foreign worker has committed administrative or penal violations during the first L permit (irregular work, labor law violations, safety infractions), the extension may be denied. Respect for the law is a fundamental condition for remaining in the canton.
### The Employer's Binding in Practice
During the L permit, the foreign worker remains legally bound to the employer declared in the original request. If the employer closes the business, ceases the activity for which the permit was granted, or terminates the worker, the L permit generally becomes ineffective. The foreign worker may receive a departure notice from the canton.
In the Canton of Schaffhausen, as in other cantons, any change in the employment situation (change of employer) requires prior approval from the authorities. A foreign worker in an L permit CANNOT leave their job and seek a new occupation autonomously: they must first obtain the approval of the new employer and a new approval from the cantonal authorities.
This binding is significantly different from permits B and C, where the worker has greater freedom to change employers as long as they remain employed and reside in the canton. If the worker is unemployed during the L permit and does not find a new authorized occupation within a reasonable period (typically 30-90 days, at the discretion of the canton), they risk expulsion from the territory.
If you need to find a new occupation, our [job search engine](nav:jobs) helps you find positions in the Canton of Schaffhausen and neighboring cantons. However, remember that any new employment relationship must be authorized by the cantonal authorities before signing the contract.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). To extend the L permit in the Canton of Schaffhausen, the employer must follow a formal procedure at the cantonal migration office, the competent authority for residence and work permits. Step 1: Check the expiry date The employer checks the exact expiry date of the L permit by consulting the original document or the cantonal administration portal. The extension request MUST be submitted at least 30-60 days before the expiry date. The timeframes vary slightly between cantons, but this is the general practice in Switzerland. A late request risks rejection. Step 2: Prepare the required documentation The employer collects the documentation according to the criteria of the cantonal office: - Extension request form (available at the Schaffhausen cantonal migration office) - Updated employment contract or letter of extension - Documentation of the employer's financial solvency and ability to pay the salary - If required: Certificate of integration of the foreigner in the canton (good conduct, regular payment of taxes, absence of administrative sanctions) Step 3: Submit the request The request is submitted to the cantonal migration office in writing or through the online portal (if available in the Canton of Schaffhausen). It is advisable to keep a copy of the request and the receipt of submission for tracking purposes. Step 4: Wait for the administrative decision The cantonal administration generally has 2-4 weeks to decide on the extension, although the timeframes may extend if additional verifications are required (labor market control, security checks, contacts with the employer). Step 5: Receive the decision If the extension is approved, the employer receives the new L permit (usually by regular mail or for pickup at the office). If rejected, the administration communicates the reasons for the rejection and the possibilities for appeal according to the cantonal procedure. ### What happens if the permit expires without extension If the L permit expires and is not extended, the foreigner generally has a term of 30 days to leave Switzerland (timeframes vary by canton). They cannot work in the Canton of Schaffhausen or remain as a resident. Continuing to work without a valid permit is a criminal offense and involves penalties for both the worker and the employer. This expiry date is categorical: there are no tacit or automatic extensions. If the L permit expires, the foreigner's situation in the canton becomes irregular. Any occupation must be immediately suspended. ### Calculate tax obligations and social contributions Use our [salary calculator](nav:calculator) to understand how your salary is subject to federal, cantonal, and municipal taxes in the Canton of Schaffhausen. As a foreigner with an L permit, direct taxes and compulsory contributions (AVS/AI, unemployment insurance, professional accident insurance, LPP where applicable) are identical to those of Swiss residents. You pay the same percentage rates on gross income. This is a critical aspect to consider in salary negotiations and economic planning for your stay in the canton.

## In a nutshell - Inheritance and gift taxes are cantonal competence in Switzerland - In the canton of Basel-Country, rates and exemptions vary depending on the degree of kinship - Spouse and direct descendants benefit from favourable treatment - The declaration of succession must be submitted within the deadlines established by the canton
## Key facts - **What**: Inheritance and gift tax, managed at cantonal level - When: The declaration must be submitted within the deadlines set by Basel Countryside - Where: Canton of Basel-Country, North-West Switzerland - Who: Beneficiaries of inheritance or grantees according to the degree of kinship - Competence: Canton (not federal government) - Variability: Different rates for each Swiss canton
In the Swiss tax system, inheritance and gift taxes remain an exclusive competence of the cantons, not the federal government. This means that each canton has the right to establish its own rules, rates and procedures, generating significant differences between regions. In the canton of Basel-Country, as in the other 25 Swiss cantons, those who inherit property or receive a donation are subject to taxation according to specific cantonal rules.
The basis of the system is the degree of kinship of the beneficiary. Not all family members pay the same tax: the spouse of the deceased, direct descendants (children, grandchildren) and other relatives are treated at rates ### Rates and degree of kinship
In the canton of Basel-Country, as in the whole of Switzerland, the inheritance tax is structured in classes of beneficiaries, each with different rights and charges, according to the general intercantonal principles. Typical categories include:
**Spouse**: In most cantons, the surviving spouse is fully exempt from inheritance tax, recognizing that the remaining spouse should not see the assets available to continue life reduced. The exemption is usually complete, regardless of the amount of the inheritance.
Direct descendants: children, grandchildren and subsequent generations benefit from progressive rates that vary depending on the blood relationship. Direct children pay less than grandchildren; grandchildren less than great-grandchildren. The intention is to promote the transfer of assets within the close family unit. Many cantons also provide exemption thresholds for descendants, i.e. amounts below which no tax is levied.
Collateral relatives: brothers, sisters, cousins and more distant relatives face higher rates according to cantonal tax rules. The farther the kinship, the higher the tax increases, reflecting the idea that a stranger's inheritance is an economic event more distant from the beneficiary.
Non-relatives: beneficiaries without blood ties (friends, non-married institutions) face the maximum, often significant, rates.

When a person dies and leaves assets in Basel-Stadt Canton, the heirs or legal representatives (executor, administrator) must declare the assets to the cantonal tax office within the established deadlines. This process is mandatory and not optional.
**Step 1: Gather Documents** The executor or principal heir must collect all relevant documentation: death certificate, will (if present), inventory of assets, bank statements, securities, and previous tax returns of the deceased. The tax office of Basel-Stadt Canton will communicate exactly which documents are required at the time of opening the inheritance.
Step 2: Submit the Declaration on Time
The deadlines for declaring inheritance are set by the canton of Basel-Stadt, typically within 90 days of death or knowledge of death. Failure to respect the deadline entails penalties and late interest, making timeliness critical. The declaration can be submitted in paper form or, in many cantons, electronically through the tax administration portal.
Step 3: Valuation and Imposition
The tax office of Basel-Stadt Canton values the inherited assets based on the criteria established by the cantonal tax law. The valuation can be made at market value, cadastral value, or according to other methods provided by the regulations. Once the taxable amount is determined, the office calculates the tax due based on the applicable rates for the beneficiary.
Step 4: Liquidation and Payment
The tax office issues a tax notice (imposition notice) specifying the amount due. The heirs generally have a specified deadline to pay (usually 30-60 days from receipt). It is possible to request payment extensions or contest the imposition before the cantonal appeal authorities if the calculation is deemed incorrect.
### Critical Deadlines and Timelines
Each phase of the procedure is governed by rigid deadlines. Failure to meet deadlines for declaration, payment, or appeal entails increasing penalties. It is essential to contact the tax office of Basel-Stadt Canton promptly at the time of inheritance and clarify the specific deadline schedule applicable.
### Where to Turn
For precise information on current rates, exemption thresholds, deadlines, and declaration procedure in Basel-Stadt Canton, it is necessary to contact the cantonal tax administration directly. Specialized lawyers in tax law and notaries can also assist in the planning and declaration process, ensuring compliance with current regulations and maximizing available exemptions.
A trusted professional will guide you through the specific details of Basel-Stadt Canton, which vary from other cantons. 4. Notary: Once all details are finalized, the parties visit the notary to sign the definitive deed (Kaufvertrag). The notary registers the deed in the cantonal land register and calculates the transfer tax.

### Transfer tax: timing and calculation
The transfer tax in the Canton Basel-Landschaft is calculated by the notary at the time of signing the definitive deed. It is a cantonal tax, meaning the rate and calculation methods are set by cantonal legislation, not federal law. The amount varies based on the purchase price and any applicable exemptions or benefits under cantonal laws, such as exemptions for the purchase of the primary residence in some cantons or reductions for spouses.
Typically, the transfer tax is paid at the time of signing the definitive deed by the notary or can be paid according to the modalities established by the canton.
### Notarial fees
Notarial fees in the Canton Basel-Landschaft are set by the notarial profession's tariff, not by federal law. They include: drafting the purchase deed, registration in the land register, legal advice, and administrative costs.
These fees are normally borne by the buyer (unless otherwise agreed with the seller) and represent, on average, 1-2% of the purchase price, depending on the complexity of the transaction.
### Additional costs: Registration fee and stamp duty
In addition to transfer tax and notarial fees, consider:
- Registration fee for the land register: A cantonal tax for registering the property in the land register.
- Valuation costs: If required by the bank for the mortgage.
- Property insurance: Mandatory if the mortgage exceeds a certain threshold. It covers property damage (fire, theft, etc.).
All these costs should be factored into the purchase planning to avoid liquidity shortfalls in the final phase.
### Final checklist before purchase
Before proceeding with the purchase, it is advisable to verify:
- Mortgage sustainability (LTV ratio, repayment capacity)
- Availability of own funds (at least 20% of the purchase price)
- Cantonal transfer tax estimate
- Notarial fee estimate
- Annual fiscal burdens as a property owner
- Property insurance coverage
Seeking the advice of a real estate consultant or notary for reviewing these aspects is highly recommended, especially if it is the first time purchasing a property in Switzerland.

## Key facts - **What**: Taxation on income, wealth and capital in the canton - Where: Canton Basel-Country (North-West Switzerland) - Who: Residents and people with income from cantonal source - Levels: Federal (IFD) + cantonal + municipal - Deductions: Professional expenses, AVS/LPP contributions, LAMal premiums according to federal law
### 3-level tax structure in the canton of Basel-Country The tax system of the Canton of Basel-Country is structured on three levels of taxation: the direct federal tax (IFD) paid to the Confederation and managed by the Federal Tax Administration (AFC), the cantonal tax administered by the regional tax office, and the municipal tax collected by the individual municipalities of the canton according to a fixed multiplier on the cantonal tax base. Each level applies progressive rates on the various brackets of taxable income, determined after the application of deductions allowed by federal legislation and specific cantonal provisions. Taxpayers resident in the canton are obliged to submit an annual tax return within the deadlines set by the cantonal administration, indicating income from employment and ### Practical implications for residents of the Canton of Basel-Country Those who reside in the canton of Basel-Country and receive income from any source are subject to taxation at all three levels: federal, cantonal and municipal. The total annual tax burden therefore depends both on the cantonal rate set by regional legislation and on the multiplier applied by the municipality of residence. Taxpayers with the same income but residing in different municipalities of the canton of Basel-Country will pay different municipal taxes, sometimes to a significant extent. For this reason, it is useful to check the municipal multiplier of your municipality and calculate the total tax burden starting from the net tax base after all allowable deductions. A preliminary estimate before the declaration makes it possible to organise the payment and assess the effect of additional deductions (e.g. voluntary payments to the third pillar 3a) on the net tax due.

## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Procedure step-by-step for the cantonal tax declaration For those residing in the Canton Basel-Landschaft and required to submit the annual declaration, the process follows these concrete steps:
**Phase 1: Collecting documentation** — Gather pay slips received, bank statements, AVS/LPP payment receipts, professional expense justifications (if self-employed), LAMal/KVG premium payment attestations during the year, documentation of donations to recognized institutions, bank account statements and investment records if subject to wealth taxation.
Phase 2: Authentication on the online portal — Reach the official website of the cantonal tax administration and authenticate with personal credentials (federal social insurance number + password, or digital signature via Swiss e-banking). The portal is available in German and French; informative texts, downloadable forms, and guides are available in Italian at the counters or upon request.
Phase 3: Filling out the declaration — Enter gross income, deduct documented expenses, indicate AVS/LPP payments made, LAMal premiums paid, and other allowed deductions. The system automatically calculates the cantonal and communal tax based on the net taxable income and applicable legislation.
Phase 4: Attaching justifications — Digitally upload required documents (pay slips, receipts, bank statements) within the file size limit set by the portal.
Phase 5: Submission and confirmation — Submit the digitally signed declaration. The portal generates a receipt with the date and time of submission; a copy remains archived in the personal account.
Phase 6: Monitoring the status — Periodically access the portal to verify the evaluation status and receive communication of the result (tax due, refund, or zero payment).
### Terms of delivery and administrative contacts The ordinary deadline for submitting the cantonal declaration is typically set between April and May of the following year of income; exact deadlines are communicated by the cantonal tax administration in documents sent to the taxpayer and visible on the official online portal. Extensions are granted upon motivated request submitted within the set terms. For clarifications on specific cantonal tax rates, allowed deductions in the canton, technical issues with accessing the portal, or other administrative matters, it is possible to contact the cantonal administration's counters in the detached capitals, the dedicated phone number for tax support (retrievable from the official website), or the email service of the tax office for non-urgent communications.
### Fiscal planning tools and tax estimates Many taxpayers use online calculators provided by federal entities (AFC) or the canton itself, where they can enter gross income and receive an accurate estimate of the total tax due (federal + cantonal + communal). Conscious fiscal planning enables taxpayers to avoid end-of-year surprises and identify legitimate opportunities for reducing their tax burden in compliance with federal and cantonal legislation.

The first concrete step is the registration in the commercial register of the canton of Basel-City. It is not an optional requirement: every economic activity exercised in a professional capacity must be registered before ### The Swiss tax system: three levels
Taxation in Switzerland consists of three distinct levels: direct federal tax (DFI), cantonal tax and municipal tax. Basel City, as a semi-canton, has its own cantonal multipliers and Basel municipalities apply municipal multipliers on a cantonal basis. This means that two businesses with the same turnover in different municipalities of Basel City can pay slightly different amounts of municipal tax, although the federal and cantonal basis remains identical.

A SAGL combines elements of both: the entity is taxed on income, but with greater distributional flexibility than an SA.

Health insurance (LAMal) is mandatory for anyone residing in Switzerland and must be taken out within 3 months of the start of residence or the start of business for those who already reside. ## Key facts - **What**: Air traffic monitoring during summer holidays - When: 26 June - 17 August 2026 - Where: Swiss airspace, Zurich and Geneva airports - Who: Skyguide (Swiss air traffic control authority) - Amount of movements: 240,108 total flights; 44,485 in Zurich, 25,514 in Geneva - Punctuality: 93% of flights on time - Delays: 63% due to weather phenomena
During the 2026 summer holidays, Swiss airspace experienced unprecedented congestion. Between June 26 and August 17, Skyguide, the federal air traffic control authority, monitored a total of 240,108 flights. A figure that reflects the strong mobility of the Swiss during the summer period.
Traffic was not uniform. The peaks were concentrated on Fridays and Mondays, when people leave for the holidays or return home. The most congested day was July 24, with 4,761 flights monitored in the national airspace. If these planes were arranged in a row, maintaining the standard distance of five nautical miles between one plane and another, the tail would reach a length greater than a full circle of the Earth.
On average, during the summer, air traffic control handled 4,503 flights per day. Two hubs have been particularly pressed: Zurich Airport What makes July 24 a day to remember in Swiss skies? The combination of factors: it is a Friday, the weekly peak, and it falls in the heart of the summer holidays when schools and companies have already closed and families move to destinations.
The distribution of almost 4,761 movements in a single day has concrete implications for those who move. Peak times — early morning and late afternoon — concentrate the bulk of take-offs. Those who fly during these times face greater risks of waiting at the gate, delays in taxiing and congestion in the cruise airspace.
### Strategies to avoid critical days
Skyguide data suggests a definite trend: Mondays and Fridays are critical-critical. If your trip allows flexibility, Tuesdays, Wednesdays, and Thursdays offer significantly less traffic. Those who evaluate alternatives, perhaps using the [trasporti pubblici](nav:transport) for destinations reachable by train, find additional travel options without air congestion.
Punctuality remains strong (93%), but 7% of delays are still relevant: on a day like July 24 with 4,761 flights, about 333 movements suffered disruptions. If you are a passenger connecting flights or have important deadlines, these numbers are worth considering.

If your trip falls in August or you are forced to fly on a Friday, here is what you can do to minimize disruptions.

item.title: Buying a house in Basel City: mortgage and costs
item.description: Practical guide to buying real estate in the canton of Basel-City: mortgage financing, transfer taxes, notary fees and step-by-step procedure. Where to inquire for specific local data.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Buying a house in Switzerland requires own funds and a mortgage regulated by the SNB - Transfer tax and notary fees are the responsibility of the canton, vary by canton and municipality - Uniform federal procedure: preliminary, financing, notarial deed, land registration
## Key facts - **What**: Purchase of residential property in Switzerland through mortgage - Who: Buyers, banks (finance mortgages), notaries (deed), Land Registry Office - Where: Canton Basel City - When: Total procedure from 4-8 weeks prior to registration - Own funds: Typically 10-20% of the purchase price (not uniform at the federal level) - Regulation: Federal mortgages (SNB); cantonal transfer taxation and land taxes
Buying a house in Basel City follows the established rules of the Swiss real estate market: a combination of private finance (own funds and mortgage loan), cantonal taxation (transfer tax) and standardized federal procedures (notarial deed, registration in the land register). Unlike in Italy, where the purchase of real estate is subject to uniform national taxes, in Switzerland the taxation on the transfer of ownership is exclusive to the cantons and municipalities. This means that the costs of a purchase in Basel City differ significantly from Zurich, Geneva or Lausanne.
Real estate financing is done through a mortgage loan: Swiss banks, subject to regulations ### Transfer tax in Switzerland: cantonal competence
The transfer tax on immovable property — also known as "transfer tax" or "registration fee" — is a tax levied on the sale of real estate. Unlike the federal direct tax (national rate) or VAT (federal competence), the transfer tax is exclusive to cantons and municipalities: each canton decides whether to introduce the tax, at what rate, and with what exemptions. The Canton of Basel City, like all Swiss cantons, has its own tax law that regulates the transfer tax. The rate varies depending on the ratio of sale price to cadastral value, as well as the type of buyer (natural person, company, entity). Some cantons exempt transfers between close relatives — parents-children, spouses — while others apply full rates.
The tax is calculated on the sale price agreed upon by the parties and recorded in the notarized deed. There is no uniform percentage: some cantons apply progressive rates (increasing with price), others fixed. The notary who draws up the deed is required to calculate the tax and notify the cantonal tax offices. A property purchased in Basel City does not incur the same rates as one purchased in Zurich or Ticino. This is why the search for the right home must take into account not only the geographical location and price, but also the local tax burden. To understand the impact of property taxes on your personal situation, consult the [tax return](nav:tax-return) and check with the Basel City cantonal tax office for specific details applicable.
### Notary fees, registration, and other costs
In addition to the transfer tax, the buyer bears non-recurring costs to complete the purchase. Notary fees — the notary's fee for drawing up the deed — are not fixed at the federal level but vary by canton and notary, as the notary market is liberalized. Typically, notary fees range from 0.5% to 1.5% of the purchase price, an estimate that requires direct consultation with local notaries in Basel City for precision.
Registration in the land register is mandatory by federal law (Swiss Civil Code, art. 960 seq.). Once the deed is drawn up, the property must be registered in the cantonal land register (Grundbuch in German). Registration fees vary: some cantons require a few dozen CHF, while others apply percentages of 0.1-0.3% of the price. Home insurance (contents and structure) is mandatory in almost every canton. The premium depends on the value of the property, geographical location, and insurance risk profile. Once the owner, the buyer pays an annual property tax (land tax), calculated on the cadastral or market value of the property. This is cantonal/municipal competence and varies significantly: some municipalities have high rates (1-2% of the value), while others are low.
### Tax deductibility: what is deductible
Are non-recurring acquisition costs deductible from taxes? It depends on Basel City legislation. Normally, notary fees and registration fees are not deductible from federal direct taxes (IFD); however, some cantons allow partial deductions from cantonal/municipal taxes. It is essential to verify with the Basel City cantonal tax office. Annual land taxes, on the other hand, are always deductible from federal direct taxes up to certain limits (standard deduction for owner-occupiers).
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Step-by-Step Procedure: How to Buy a House in Switzerland
The procedure for buying a property in Switzerland follows a standardized federal path, with cantonal variations:
**1. Search and Preliminary Offer** Identify the desired house, the buyer makes a verbal or written offer. The price is completely negotiable. If the seller accepts the offer, the parties sign a non-binding preliminary agreement or a memorandum of sale outlining the main terms.
2. Financing: Bank Approval The buyer contacts one or more Swiss banks (the market is competitive: request quotes from 3-4 institutions) for a mortgage offer. The bank requires: ID and proof of residence, last 2-3 pay stubs, tax return, bank statement to verify available assets, independent property inspection, and registry certificate. After 2-3 weeks of evaluation, the bank issues a mortgage offer with an indicative interest rate, term, maximum amount, and explicit sustainability conditions.
3. Resolution and Notarial Deed Upon bank approval, the buyer and seller agree on a notarization date (usually 4-8 weeks after offer acceptance). The notary drafts the sale deed with public signature, describing the cadastral data, agreed price, payment methods, and mortgage charge (the mortgage pledge). The parties sign in the presence of the notary.
4. Payment and Property Transfer The bank transfers the mortgage to the seller's lawyer or notary's account. The buyer pays their own funds. The notary verifies the total balance and authorizes the property transfer.
5. Registration in the Land Registry The notary files the deed with the Basel City Land Registry Office. Registration (within 1-2 weeks) perfects the transfer: the buyer is officially the owner, registered in the local Grundbuch.
6. Insurance and Tax Management The buyer takes out a house insurance policy (contents and structure), registers the property with the cantonal or municipal tax office for annual land tax payment, and requests connection to utilities (gas, electricity, water).
### Where to Inform Yourself in Basel City
To acquire specific information on prices, taxes, procedures, and local requirements:
- Basel City Land Registry Office: provides verified cadastral extracts and property information - Basel City Tax Office: explains transfer taxes, land taxes, and local deductions - Basel City Notaries (professional association): provides precise quotes on notarial fees and operational guides on the procedure - Swiss banks operating in the canton: UBS, Credit Suisse, Raiffisen, and others provide mortgage quotes and advice on sustainability - Licensed real estate agents: provide market reports, indicative valuations, and local market information
The [mortgage calculator](nav:calculator) available on this website helps you estimate the monthly payment and mortgage sustainability based on own funds, mortgage amount, and indicative interest rate. For further information on the Swiss pension system and the impact of property ownership on your future income, read the guide to [pillar 3](nav:pillar3). ### How costs affect disposable income
Suppose a household with a gross monthly income of CHF 10,000. If the custodial fee absorbs CHF 2,000 per month, the disposable income is reduced to CHF 8,000 before taxation. item.title: Permit C Basel City: rights and naturalization requirements
item.description: Residence permit C in the Canton of Basel City: 10 years residence (5 EU/EFTA), federal integration, cantonal procedure and path to Swiss ordinary naturalization.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - The C permit is the federal permanent residence permit for foreigners in Switzerland - Minimum requirement: 10 years continuous residence (5 for EU/EFTA citizens) - Basel City manages local integration procedure and criteria according to federal law - Permit C paves the way towards ordinary Swiss naturalisation
## Key facts - **What**: Residence permit C (federal permanent residence permit) - When: Release normally after ≥10 years residence (5 for EU/EFTA) - Where: Canton Basel City (cantonal competence for procedure and integration) - Who: Federal SEM Administration + cantonal authorities Basel City - Requirements: Continuous residence, absence of public safety hazards, basic integration
Residence permit C is the most important federal title for foreigners who wish to settle permanently in Switzerland. At the national level, federal law normally provides for issuance after 10 years of continuous residence, or after 5 years for citizens of the European Union and the European Free Trade Association (EFTA). In the Canton of Basel-City, as in all Swiss cantons, this federal competence is administered in synergy with cantonal requirements, which include integration criteria and compliance with local regulations.
Permit C represents the fundamental step towards lasting legal stability: it allows unlimited residence, facilitates access to the labour market without ### Cantonal procedure in Basel-City: how it works
In the Canton of Basel-City, the C permit is administered by the competent cantonal migration office (part of the cantonal police structure or department of justice). The application is not automatic: after meeting the minimum residency requirement, the resident foreign national must submit a formal application to the local authorities.
The cantonal procedure, although following federal principles, includes specific verification steps: the cantonal administration checks municipal registries to certify 10 years (or 5 for EU/EFTA) of uninterrupted residency. Subsequently, the SEM and cantonal authorities verify whether the applicant has a clean criminal record and does not pose a security threat. Basel-City, like other cantons, evaluates integration through specific criteria: knowledge of German (the official language of the canton), participation in the labor market, and absence of dependence on social welfare. Following complete verification, the canton issues the C permit, normally valid for 10 years and renewable.
Generally, the procedure takes between 3 and 6 months, depending on the cantonal administrative workload. Federal law provides for cases of early issuance: the C permit may be granted before 10 years (or 5 for EU/EFTA) in special situations such as marriage to a Swiss citizen (required residency reduced to 3-5 years in cantons that allow it), children of Swiss citizens (more favorable criteria), or employees of companies of federal significance (rarely). Basel-City may apply these exceptions, but the details remain in the hands of the local cantonal administration.
### What changes in life after the C permit
With the C permit, you gain access to rights that the B permit (temporary residence) does not grant: complete freedom of movement (you can change canton or city of residence without prior authorization, although you must register with local authorities). Access to the labor market becomes unlimited: no professional restrictions; you can look for work in any sector. Social rights expand: access to cantonal social subsidies and benefits, although with some limitations based on citizenship and duration of residency. For the [tax return](nav:tax-return) and other fiscal aspects, your permanent residence is legally recognized at the federal level, simplifying procedures and transparency. Finally, social security contributions become mandatory: you contribute to AVS/AHV (old-age and survivors insurance) and AI (disability insurance) with a rate of 5.3% for employees (10.6% total including the employer). If employed, LPP/BVG (occupational pension insurance) with a variable rate (7% between 25-34 years, 10% between 35-44 years, 15% between 45-54 years, 18% from 55 years until the reference age) also becomes binding.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Step-by-step procedure to apply for a C permit in Basel-City
**Step 1: Check the prerequisites**. Ensure you have reached 10 years of uninterrupted residency in Switzerland (or 5 if you are an EU/EFTA citizen). Check your municipal registry for the exact registration date and keep official documentation.
Step 2: Gather documentation. You will need to submit a valid passport or identity card, criminal record extracts (from your country of origin and Switzerland, if applicable), a recently issued municipal residence certificate, an employment document (employment contract) or tax return, and proof of language proficiency (diplomas, certificates, or a simple declaration, depending on the canton of Basel-City practice).
Step 3: Contact the competent office. The exact address depends on the cantonal administration of Basel-City. Generally, it is the Cantonal Police (Department of Justice and Security) or a specific immigration office. Check the official portal of the canton.
Step 4: Submit the application. It can be submitted in person at the office, by mail, or via the cantonal online portal (if available).
Step 5: Wait for verification. The canton will carry out residency, security, and integration checks. Remain available for any interviews or requests for additional documents. It is normal to receive requests for clarification during this period.
Step 6: Receive the issuance. Once approved, you will receive the C permit in the form of a federal legitimization card or digital document according to cantonal procedures.
### The path to ordinary Swiss naturalization
Residency permit C paves the way for ordinary Swiss naturalization, which represents the next step for those wishing to acquire Swiss citizenship. At the federal level, the minimum requirements are: possession of permit C, at least 10 years of residency in Switzerland (with favorable counting: years between 18 and 22 count double, reducing the effective time). However, naturalization is not a completely automatic federal procedure: each canton and sometimes each municipality has its own procedures and criteria. In Basel-City, as elsewhere, the procedure generally takes 6-18 months and may include in-depth historical, civic, or language knowledge tests.
To learn more about how permit C impacts your tax and social security position in Switzerland, consult the [salary calculator](nav:calculator), which helps you understand the impact of federal, cantonal, and municipal taxation on your gross income. To check how OASI (AVS) and occupational pension (LPP) work after the issuance of permit C, access the [social security guide](nav:pension).

item.title: Residence permit B Basel City: requirements and renewal
item.description: Practical guide to the renewable residence permit in the Canton of Basel-City: requirements, documents, duration, renewal procedure and contacts of the migration office.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Permit B = renewable stay for foreigners in Switzerland - Each canton has autonomy over requirements and procedures - Basel City manages the release through cantonal migration office - Different from permit L (short duration) and C (domicile)
## Key facts - **What**: Residence permit category B (renewable) - Where: Canton of Basel-City, north-western Switzerland - Who: Basel City Cantonal Migration Office - Type: SEM category B - Duration: Renewable (specific for canton)
In the Canton of Basel-City, the category B residence permit represents the renewable residence permit for foreigners wishing to settle in Switzerland. Managed by the cantonal migration office, this permit is part of the SEM system that regulates the entry and stay of foreign nationals throughout Switzerland. Unlike other residence permits, the B permit is characterised by its renewability, allowing those who hold it to extend their residence permit at the end of its validity.
### Permit B in the Swiss SEM system
In Switzerland, the stay of foreigners is regulated by the SEM permit system, which provides for four main categories. The L permit is intended for those who intend to stay for a short period, up to one year. The B permit, on the other hand, is designed for those who want a more stable and continuous residence, with characteristic renewability. Then there is permit C, intended Permit B vs permit C: practical differences
Those who plan to move to Switzerland often ask which type of permit is more suitable for their situation. The main differences between the permit of residence (category B) and the permit of domicile (category C) are significant both on the administrative and practical planes.
The permit B is renewable for limited periods and must be requested for renewal. The permit C, on the other hand, is intended for those who have accumulated a minimum period of residence in Switzerland: generally not less than 10 years for citizens of non-EU/EEA countries, and not less than 5 years for citizens of the European Union and the European Free Trade Association. The permit C confers a more stable position and does not require periodic renewals in the same way.
Even from the point of view of geographical mobility, the two categories differ. The holder of a permit B must generally notify changes of domicile within the canton, and must renew the permit if they decide to move to another canton. The holder of a permit C has greater freedom of movement within Switzerland.
From the point of view of access to social services and healthcare, both permit B and C holders have the right to coverage of [LAMal (mandatory health insurance)](nav:health), which is a private insurance with premiums per capita. In the Canton of Basel City, as in all cantons, LAMal is mandatory for all residents within 3 months of arrival. Cantonally subsidized premiums for reducing premiums vary by canton and individual situation.
### Fiscal and pension implications
From a tax perspective, both permit B and C holders are subject to the Swiss three-tier tax system: federal direct tax (managed by AFC/ESTV), cantonal tax, and municipal tax. Each canton has its own rates and regulations, and municipalities apply a multiplier to cantonal tax. In the Canton of Basel City, specific rates must be checked with the competent cantonal tax administration.
Regarding social security, permit B holders who work in Switzerland are enrolled in the AVS/AI (old-age and disability insurance) system. Contributions are 5.3% for the employee and 10.6% in total with the employer. In addition, employees are subject to contributions for unemployment insurance (AD/AC), amounting to 1.1% up to an annual maximum.
Regarding the company pension fund (LPP/BVG), permit B holders who earn a coordinated salary have compulsory contributions that vary by age range: 7% for the 25-34 age range, 10% for 35-44 years, 15% for 45-54 years, and 18% for 55 years up to the reference age. These contributions are deducted directly from the salary.
### Family allocations and social rights
An important aspect concerns access to family allocations. Permit B holders who work in Switzerland and have children can access family allocations, the amount of which varies by canton. In addition, the permit B holder has the right to 2 weeks of paid leave for paternity insurance (federal right).
As for the insurance against work-related accidents (LAINF/LAA), this is mandatory for employees with permit B and amounts to around 0.7-1.5% of the salary depending on the sector. Insurance against occupational diseases is part of the same coverage.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### How to Apply for a B Permit in Basel City: Procedures and Deadlines
Those wishing to relocate to the Canton of Basel City must follow a clear administrative procedure. The first step is to complete the application form provided by the cantonal migration office of Basel City. This form must be accompanied by the required documentation (identity document, residence certificate, police certificate, and any income documentation).
Once the application is submitted, the cantonal migration office examines the request and verifies compliance with the requirements. The processing time typically ranges from a few days to several weeks, depending on the complexity of the application and the office's workload. It is recommended to maintain regular contact with the office to check the status of the application.
After approval of the application, the B permit is issued with a validity and expiration date. The permit holder receives an official copy, which must be carefully preserved, as it is the document that attests the right to stay in Switzerland.
### Permit Renewal: Timelines and Documents
The renewal of the residence permit (category B) must be requested before the expiration date. Normally, the Canton of Basel City sends a reminder to the permit holder a few months before the expiration date, reminding them to renew. However, it is the permit holder's responsibility to check the expiration date on the permit.
To renew, you must:
- Submit a renewal request within the times set by the canton - Provide updated documentation (residence certificate, police certificate, and any income documentation) - Pay any applicable administrative renewal fee - Verify that the original conditions persist (residence in the canton, compliance with the law)
If the conditions persist and there are no issues with the application, the permit is renewed, and a new copy is issued valid for the next period.
### Contacts and Information at the Cantonal Migration Office
The cantonal migration office of Basel City is the primary point of contact for any questions related to the B permit. It is recommended to contact the office to verify specific requirements, obtain the updated list of required documents, know the submission deadlines, receive assistance in completing the application, and clarify any doubts about the renewal procedure.
Cantonal migration offices operate according to fixed opening hours and usually offer the possibility of phone, email, or in-person contact. It is recommended to check the contact details and hours before visiting the office.
### Support Tools: Fiscal and Social Security Information
Once the B permit is obtained, the permit holder must fulfill obligations such as registration with the local municipality and enrollment in the tax system. At the federal level, the Federal Administration of Customs and the Federal Tax Administration (ESTV) manage the federal direct tax and VAT. At the cantonal level (at the Basel City Tax Administration), practical compliance with cantonal and municipal taxes is managed.
Regarding social security, it is essential to verify enrollment in the AVS system at the Social Insurance Office (UFAS/BSV) and enrollment in the occupational pension fund (LPP) at the employer or relevant pension fund.
To verify your fiscal and income situation in Switzerland once the B permit is obtained, [calculate your net salary](nav:calculator). Fiscal and social security burdens are essential components of financial planning in Basel City Canton.

In the Canton of Solothurn, as in every Swiss canton, the labour market reflects a professional structure based on training levels and pay levels defined by federal law and cantonal ordinances. The search for employment and the determination of salaries follow precise rules that directly affect the paycheck, social security contributions and compulsory insurance.
### Salary bands by degree of training
The Swiss employment market is historically divided into three levels of qualification. The first is vocational apprenticeship (AFC — Federal Certificate ### Mandatory Contributions and Insurance Obligations
A worker's salary in the Canton of Solothurn consists of a gross part (the contractual salary) and a series of mandatory deductions. These reflect federal, cantonal contributions and insurance obligations established by Swiss laws.
**First Pillar: AVS/AI/IPG
The Old Age and Survivors Insurance (AVS), Disability Insurance (AI), and Maternity/Paternity Loss of Earnings Indemnity (IPG) constitute the first pillar of Swiss pension provision. The dependent worker pays 5.3% of the gross salary; the employer pays 10.6% in total (with its own share of 5.3%). These contributions finance public pensions: from 64 years for women (65 for men), the worker receives a monthly AVS pension based on contributions paid and years of work.
Unemployment
Unemployment contributions (AD — Unemployment Insurance; AC — Unemployment Insurance for the Worker's Fault) total 1.1% up to a yearly maximum, divided between the dependent and the employer. These payments ensure a daily allowance if the worker loses their job involuntarily.
Accidents at Work Insurance
The Work Accidents Insurance (LAINF) is paid by the employer to an insurance company (SUVA or recognized private insurers) and varies from 0.7% to 1.5% depending on the activity sector. The employee does not contribute directly; the employer includes the cost in the operational budget.
### Second Pillar: Occupational Pension (LPP/BVG)
The Pension Fund (LPP — Law on Occupational Pension for Old Age, Survivors, and Disability) is mandatory for employees with an annual salary above a coordinated threshold (not included in this analysis, as it is annually indexed). The LPP operates on a defined contribution basis: the employer pays a percentage of the coordinated salary (gross salary minus a deduction), the employee another percentage. The rates increase with age:
- Age 25–34 years: 7% - Age 35–44 years: 10% - Age 45–54 years: 15% - Age 55+ up to the reference age (65 men, 64 women): 18%
These percentages apply to the coordinated salary, not the entire salary. The LPP accumulates individual capital during working life, paid out as a monthly pension at retirement or as a lump sum (according to the fund's choices).
### LAMal: Mandatory Health Insurance
Every resident in Switzerland must subscribe to a mandatory health insurance (LAMal/KVG) within 3 months of arrival or starting work. Unlike AVS, LPP, and unemployment contributions, LAMal IS NOT a salary contribution. item.description: Swiss wage system by level of training and sector. Collective agreements, where the cantonal minimum wage exists and how to calculate the net from the paycheck.

## In Brief - No federal minimum wage; some cantons have their own - Maximum working hours: 45 hours/week (industry, offices), 50 hours other sectors - Collective contracts determine minimum wages for professional categories - AVS/AI contributions: 5.3% employee, employer adds 10.6% total
## Key Facts - **What**: Swiss salary structure regulated by training, sector, and collective contracts - When: Current system in place - Where: Nationwide Switzerland, all cantons including Solothurn - Who: SECO (Federal Department of Economic Affairs), UST/BFS (Federal Statistical Office), unions, employers - Working hours: Max 45 hours industry/offices, 50 hours other sectors - Vacations: Minimum 4 weeks annual leave; 5 weeks if under 20 - Maternity: 14 weeks at 80% with loss of earnings compensation (LEC) ### How salaries vary by level of education The level of education is the most significant factor in determining the initial salary and career progression in Switzerland. An apprentice who has completed an AFC in a craft profession earns a fraction of the salary of a high school diploma holder, who in turn earns less than a university graduate in the same field. The wage differential is substantial and is also reflected in the final pension calculated through the Professional Pension Foundation (LPP).
Swiss cantons periodically publish data on average salaries by level of education, compiled by SECO and UST/BFS at the federal level. However, specific data for Solothurn should be consulted with the cantonal administration or local chambers of commerce.
### Sectors and salary prospects The main sectors of the Swiss economy include manufacturing industry (metal and chemical), financial services, retail and wholesale trade, hospitality and catering, healthcare, education, and public administration. Each sector has its own collective agreements, and salaries vary significantly: financial services have higher average salaries than retail trade. At the national level, SECO and UST/BFS periodically publish statistics on average salaries by sector.
### Mandatory contributions and net pay A critical aspect often overlooked is the difference between the contractual gross salary and the actual net salary. Mandatory contributions include: - **AVS/AI/IPG** (Old-age, disability, and loss of earnings insurance): 5.3% of the gross salary of the employee; the employer adds a share of 10.6% in total - Unemployment insurance (AD) and costs of unemployment benefit insurance (AC): 1.1% up to annual maximum - Accident insurance (LAINF/LAA): 0.7-1.5% depending on the sector of work - LPP (Professional Pension Foundation): varies from 7% (age 25-34) to 18% (55+ until reference age) on coordinated salary
In addition to these 'collective mandatory' contributions, the employee also pays federal, cantonal, and municipal taxes. In the Canton of Solothurn, cantonal and municipal taxes are determined by local administrations; federal direct tax (IFD) is set by federal legislation. Health insurance (LAMal) is mandatory for all Swiss residents, but IT IS NOT a salary contribution — it is a privately stipulated premium with a health insurance fund, variable by canton and age group.

The coordinated salary: In your pay slip, your employer will indicate the coordinated salary, which is used to calculate LPP contributions. It is not necessarily the same as the gross contractual salary. 3. Working hours and vacations: Check that the contract clearly specifies the weekly working hours (maximum 45 hours industry/offices, 50 hours other sectors) and the number of annual leave days (minimum 4 weeks, 5 if you are under 20 years old). 4. Benefits and allowances: Some CCs provide thirteenth salaries, bonuses, transportation allowances, or company contributions to health insurance. Ask your employer explicitly. 5. Termination and notice periods: The ordinary notice period is 1 month during the first year of employment, 2 months from the second to the ninth year, and 3 months from the tenth year of service.

An apparent paradox characterises the Swiss flat-rate taxation market: the number of wealthy foreigners opting for this regime is visibly falling, yet the cantons are collecting more and more money. Ticino perfectly embodies this contradiction. In 2024 it collected 189.5 million francs in total (federal, cantonal and municipal taxes), 71 million more than in 2016. The flat-rate taxation scheme, which was established on Lake Geneva in the 1920s to attract wealthy foreigners residing in Switzerland, is based on annual expenditure. The calculation takes into account the cost of living, which includes expenses for accommodation, cars, travel and other consumption. For federal tax the minimum taxable income is set at CHF 435,000. For those who own their own home, the threshold is at least seven times the annual rent or rental value of the property. The cantons also set their own thresholds, often different from the federal level.
Most flat-rate taxpayers come from Europe. In the Valais there are mainly French, English, Belgian, Dutch and Italian citizens. In Zug, about a quarter comes from Germany.
